method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: The dollar slipped to a one-month low on Monday, near 101.45 on its index, as falling oil and hopes of a deal to end the Iran war pulled shelter money back out. Two Federal Reserve officials still say rates need to rise, so Tuesday's midterm elections and Friday's October jobs report decide whether that support comes back.

EUR.text: The euro jumped to about $1.123 on Monday as the dollar weakened and oil fell, and euro-zone factories kept growing in October with costs rising fast, which backs the European Central Bank's hint of a December rate rise. France is the weak spot: its economy shrank and Fitch warned it may cut the country's credit rating, while German gas stores start winter short of target.

GBP.text: The pound sits near $1.345 and at its strongest against the euro this year, and British factories just had their best month for output in two years with prices rising faster. Economists expect the Bank of England to lift its rate from 3.75% to 4% on Thursday, November 5, its first rise since 2023, so a hold or a split vote would likely knock the pound.

JPY.text: The Bank of Japan held its rate at 1.25% on Friday but said underlying inflation has reached its 2% goal, and one board member wanted a rise straight away, so a December hike looks likely. Monday's fall in oil helps Japan, which buys almost all its energy abroad, and Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama repeated that Tokyo will act against wild yen swings, though the yen still sits near 157.6 per dollar.

CHF.text: The Swiss franc draws shelter money when stocks fall, as in Friday's worst US stock day since June, and talk of possible new US strikes on Iran adds to that. But Washington now says no decision on strikes has been made and talks continue, and Swiss rates far below US rates also pull the other way.

CAD.text: The Bank of Canada raised its rate to 2.5% last week, its first hike in three years, and high oil prices have helped the loonie. But oil fell sharply on Monday on hopes of an end to the Iran war, figures show Canada's economy stalled, and a US-Canada trade deal that President Trump calls very close would help only if it brings tariff cuts.

AUD.text: The Reserve Bank of Australia is widely expected to raise its rate to 4.85% on Tuesday, November 3, its fifth rise this year, which supports the Australian dollar near 70 US cents. But much of that is priced in, many economists think it will be the last rise, and China, Australia's biggest customer, sent mixed signals from its factory surveys; a hold would likely hit the currency.

NZD.text: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised by keeping its rate at 2.75% on October 28 instead of raising it, so the kiwi has lost its rate support and sits near 56 US cents. Weaker-than-expected Chinese business surveys, a key market for New Zealand's dairy, add to the drag.

XAU.text: Gold fell to its lowest in a year on Friday, below $3,900 an ounce, as Fed officials talked up more rate rises and some investors sold it to cover stock losses. It bounced about 1% on Monday as markets calmed, but the chance of a December US rate rise still weighs on it.

OIL.text: Brent crude ended October at a six-month high but fell about 4% on Monday, to near $110 a barrel, after President Trump signalled more time for talks and an official said a draft US-Iran deal is circulating. Ships are still being hit in and near the Strait of Hormuz and Iran wants the US blockade lifted first, so the drop could reverse fast if talks stall after Tuesday's US midterm elections.

items.headline: Iranians have left Doha talks, draft proposal for US deal being circulated, official says
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Iran's negotiators have left the Qatar-hosted talks with the US, but an official says a draft deal to end the war is now being passed around and another meeting may follow.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since late February. Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, mostly shut, and the US has blockaded Iran's ports. Qatar has been carrying messages between the two sides.
beats.happened: An official briefed on the talks said Iran's team left Doha, Qatar's capital, on Sunday, not because the talks broke down, and that a draft agreement is circulating, without giving details. Esmaeil Baghaei, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman, said there can be no final deal or reopening of Hormuz until the US blockade ends.
beats.means: This is the first sign of an actual text on the table, which supports the hope behind Monday's fall in oil. But Iran's conditions are steep, and President Trump has said he still has one or two targets in Iran, while promising no strikes before Tuesday's midterm elections.
beats.fx: Talk of a deal weighs on oil and on the dollar's shelter demand; it hurts oil sellers like Canada and helps big energy buyers like Japan and the euro zone.

impact.why: A draft deal makes a reopening of Hormuz more likely, but nothing is agreed and no details are known.
Cheaper oil would cut Canada's export income.
Japan imports almost all its energy, so lower oil eases its import bill.

items.watch: Whether a second round of talks is set, and whether the US eases its blockade; any new strike after Tuesday's vote would undo the hope.

items.headline: Dollar pulls back ahead of US midterms; bitcoin stabilises after crypto heist
items.story_title: US midterms: a week of elections, central banks and jobs data
items.summary: The dollar slipped to its weakest in a month on Monday and the euro jumped about 0.7% to near $1.123, as cheaper oil and calmer markets eased demand for the US currency.

beats.was: The dollar had been propped up by high oil prices, fear around the Iran war and Federal Reserve officials calling for higher US rates. Americans vote in midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, and the Bank of England, the Reserve Bank of Australia and the central banks of Norway and Sweden all decide on rates this week.
beats.happened: The dollar index fell about 0.5% to roughly 101.45, a one-month low. The euro rose to about $1.123 even though Fitch had just warned it may cut France's credit rating, the pound edged up to about $1.345, and the yen held near 157.6 per dollar. Brent crude fell almost 4% on hopes the US-Iran war can be ended by talks. Bitcoin steadied near $78,000 after hackers stole $6.3 billion from the crypto exchange Binance last week, a theft the FBI blames on North Korea.
beats.means: With oil falling and fear easing, some of the shelter money that had gone into the dollar is flowing back out. Kit Juckes, head of currency strategy at Société Générale, pointed to better risk mood and lower oil as the weight on the dollar.
beats.fx: A softer dollar lifts the euro and pound most; the yen and Australian dollar barely moved ahead of their own news.

impact.why: Cheaper oil and calmer markets cut demand for the dollar as a safe place, taking it to a one-month low.
The euro had its best start to a week in a while, shrugging off the warning on France's credit rating.
A small gain against a weaker dollar ahead of Thursday's Bank of England decision.

items.watch: Tuesday's midterm results and Friday's October US jobs report; renewed fighting in the Gulf would likely send money back into the dollar.

items.headline: Oil prices slide more than 3% as Trump signals more time for Iran diplomacy
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Oil fell more than 3% on Monday, with Brent near $110 a barrel, after reports that President Trump wants to give talks with Iran more time before any new US strikes.

beats.was: Brent crude rose about 15% in October to a six-month high as attacks on Gulf shipping and talk of fresh US strikes on Iran raised fears for supply. Iranian officials have been meeting go-betweens in Qatar about ending the war.
beats.happened: Brent dropped to about $110 and US crude to about $101. Axios reported that Trump told Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, he wanted diplomacy to run longer before weighing more strikes, and Trump said on Sunday the war would end soon one way or another. Ships were still being hit near the Strait of Hormuz and off Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast over the weekend.
beats.means: The market is pricing a better chance of a deal and a smaller chance of new strikes this week, but the attacks at sea show supply is still at risk. The bank UBS still sees Brent near $110 at year-end.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil helps big energy buyers such as Japan and the euro zone and takes some support from oil exporters such as Canada and Norway.

impact.why: Signs Washington will hold off on new strikes cut the war premium in prices.
Lower oil trims support for Canada's main export.
A cheaper energy bill eases a long-running drag on Japan's trade balance.
The euro zone imports most of its energy, so lower oil helps.

items.watch: Whether the Qatar talks yield a plan to reopen Hormuz, and what Washington says about strikes once Tuesday's vote is over.

items.headline: Oil slips more than 1% as talks continue on ending Iran war
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Oil fell about 1.5% as trading opened in Asia on Monday, with Brent near $112 a barrel, as Iran and Qatar held a third day of talks on ending the war.

beats.was: Brent crude ended October at a six-month high after weeks of attacks on Gulf shipping, and the US has said it may strike Iran again. Qatar is acting as go-between for Washington and Tehran.
beats.happened: Brent fell $1.59 to about $111.84 and US crude to about $102.56 early Monday. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said the talks in Doha were progressing, and a quiet weekend with no major military escalation took some urgency out of prices; OPEC+ also kept December output targets unchanged.
beats.means: The market is shaving a little of the war premium on hopes of a deal, but it remains nervous that fighting could resume after Tuesday's US midterm elections.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil eases the import bill for Japan and Europe and takes a little support away from oil exporters such as Canada.

impact.why: Hopes for a deal to end the war pulled prices well off last week's highs at the open.
Lower oil trims support for Canada's biggest export.
A smaller energy bill helps Japan, which buys nearly all its oil abroad.

items.watch: Whether the Doha talks produce a plan to reopen Hormuz, and what Washington says about strikes after Tuesday's vote.

items.headline: Tanker hit by two projectiles off Saudi coast as Gulf incidents reach 10 in three days
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: A tanker was struck by two unidentified projectiles in the northern Gulf off Saudi Arabia early Monday, the tenth reported attack on shipping in the region since Saturday.

beats.was: Since the US-Israeli war on Iran began, ships in and near the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel that carries about a fifth of the world's oil, have been hit by mines, drones and missiles. Iran's Revolutionary Guards have claimed several of these attacks.
beats.happened: The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre, which tracks shipping security for the Royal Navy, said a tanker sailing southeast was hit on its side about 72 nautical miles east of Ras Al Khafji, near the Saudi-Kuwaiti border. All crew are safe and no spill was reported; the ship and the attacker were not named.
beats.means: The attacks are no longer limited to the strait itself but reach the northern Gulf, where Saudi and Kuwaiti crude is loaded. That tends to lift insurance and freight costs even while talks to end the war continue in Qatar.
beats.fx: More risk to Gulf shipping supports oil prices, which helps oil exporters like Canada and Norway and hurts big importers such as Japan and the euro zone.

impact.why: A new attack further up the Gulf adds to supply risk, but no damage to oil flows was reported and prices stayed lower on the day.
Japan imports almost all its oil, so pricier shipping through the Gulf is a cost for its economy.

items.watch: Whether anyone claims the attack, and whether tanker traffic out of Saudi and Kuwaiti ports slows.

items.headline: China private factory PMI at 52.0 beats forecasts, output growth fastest since April
items.story_title: China: a slowing economy
items.summary: A private survey of Chinese factories came in at 52.0 for October, better than the 51.6 expected, with output growing at its fastest pace in six months.

beats.was: China's official factory survey, released on Saturday, showed activity shrinking in October (49.3, below the 50 line that splits growth from decline), which had raised worries about Australia's and New Zealand's biggest customer.
beats.happened: The RatingDog survey, compiled by S&P Global and tilted toward exporters, slipped only slightly from 52.1 in September. Output and buying picked up, but export orders grew at their slowest in three months, factories cut selling prices, and business confidence fell to a nine-month low.
beats.means: China's private exporters are holding up better than the official numbers suggest, which eases fears of a sharp slowdown. Falling factory prices still point to weak demand at home and keep pressure on Beijing to add support.
beats.fx: Better Chinese factory activity gives some relief to currencies tied to China's demand, mainly the Australian and New Zealand dollars.

impact.why: A beat from Australia's biggest customer softens Saturday's weak official survey, though the mix inside is soft.
Steadier Chinese factories help demand for New Zealand's exports a little.

items.watch: China's services survey later this week, and whether Beijing's market regulators announce support after meeting banks on Monday.

items.headline: Japan's Katayama says US-Japan FX statement 'alive', warns on disorderly yen moves
items.story_title: Japan: guarding the yen near 160 per dollar
items.summary: Japan's finance minister said Tokyo's currency pact with Washington still stands whatever happens in Tuesday's US midterm elections, and that Japan will step in against wild swings in the yen.

beats.was: The yen has been weak all year and slid close to 160 per dollar, a level where Japan has sold dollars to prop it up before. Japan and the US agreed a joint statement on currencies that accepts action against disorderly moves.
beats.happened: Satsuki Katayama, Japan's finance minister, said on Monday that the joint statement is still in force and that the two governments will stay aligned after the US vote. She would not judge the yen's current level, but said markets are calmer than before and that Japan will act against disorderly or speculative moves.
beats.means: The warning is a reminder that Tokyo is still watching, which puts a soft ceiling on how far the dollar can climb against the yen. But she sounded less urgent than when the yen was near 160, so this is a standing guard, not a sign of action soon.
beats.fx: It mildly supports the yen by keeping the threat of Japanese buying alive, and limits the dollar's room to rise against it.

impact.why: Repeats a known warning; it keeps a floor under the yen but adds no new pressure.
Caps how far the dollar can rise against the yen while the threat of action stands.

items.watch: How fast the dollar moves against the yen around Tuesday's US vote and Friday's jobs report; a quick run back toward 160 is what would bring sharper words or action.

items.headline: Market Quick Take - Markets find calm after Friday turmoil - 2 November 2026
items.story_title: Gold: sliding as Fed rate-rise bets build
items.summary: Gold bounced about 1% to near $3,915 an ounce early Monday after Friday's drop to its lowest in a year, as markets calmed after the worst US stock day since June.

beats.was: Gold fell almost 7% in October and broke below $3,900 on Friday, hit by talk of more US rate rises and by investors selling it to cover losses in technology stocks.
beats.happened: Saxo Bank's morning note shows gold up about 1% to roughly $3,915 and silver up about 2% to near $50.20 early Monday, with stock markets in Asia steadier and oil about 3% lower.
beats.means: This is a small recovery from forced selling, not a turn: the main weight on gold, the chance of a Federal Reserve rate rise in December, has not gone away.
beats.fx: A softer dollar on Monday helps gold a little; Friday's US jobs report matters most for the next big move.

impact.why: A modest bounce after a sharp fall as panic selling eased.

items.watch: Friday's October US jobs report; strong hiring would revive bets on a December Fed rate rise and pressure gold again.

items.headline: Eurozone manufacturing growth holds steady in October
items.story_title: Euro zone: growth holding up, prices still rising
items.summary: Euro-zone factories kept growing in October for a ninth month, though a bit more slowly, while their costs rose at the fastest pace since May.

beats.was: The European Central Bank hinted last week it could raise rates in December, after the euro zone grew faster than expected last quarter. A purchasing managers' index (PMI) reading above 50 means activity is growing.
beats.happened: S&P Global's final euro-zone manufacturing PMI for October came in at 52.7, down from 52.9 in September. Output grew at its slowest in four months, but exports rose at the quickest pace in over four years. Input costs climbed at the fastest rate since May and selling prices kept rising sharply. France and Italy were the only big members where factories shrank.
beats.means: Industry is holding up, helped by defence spending and firms building stock, and the rise in costs keeps pressure on the ECB to act on prices.
beats.fx: Steady factory growth with firmer prices backs the case for a December ECB hike, mildly supportive for the euro.

impact.why: Solid factory growth and rising costs keep a December ECB rate rise on the table.

items.watch: Wednesday's flash euro-zone inflation figure for October; a softer reading would cool the hike talk.

items.headline: UK manufacturing PMI rises to 52.8 in October
items.story_title: Bank of England: first rate rise since 2023?
items.summary: British factories had their best month in two years for output in October, and their selling prices rose at the fastest pace in three months, days before an expected Bank of England rate rise.

beats.was: Economists expect the Bank of England to lift its rate from 3.75% to 4% on Thursday, November 5, its first rise since 2023, because price pressures are building. A purchasing managers' index (PMI) reading above 50 means activity is growing.
beats.happened: S&P Global's UK manufacturing PMI rose to 52.8 in October from 51.9, a five-month high. Production grew at its fastest pace in 25 months and new orders picked up at home and abroad. Input costs rose at one of the sharpest rates in four years, factory prices climbed faster, and hiring stalled. Shipping detours and conflict-related disruption slowed deliveries.
beats.means: Firm demand plus rising costs fits the case for a Bank of England hike this week rather than against it.
beats.fx: Supports the pound by making a Thursday rate rise look safer.

impact.why: Stronger factory activity and faster price rises back the expected rate rise on Thursday.

items.watch: Thursday's Bank of England decision and how many policymakers vote to raise rates.

items.headline: Trump Says U.S. and Canada 'Very Close' to Trade Deal, Carney Cites Constructive Talks
items.story_title: US-Canada trade: tariffs and talks
items.summary: President Trump told an Iowa rally on Sunday that the US and Canada are very close to a trade deal that would include the Keystone XL oil pipeline, while Prime Minister Mark Carney said talks will take weeks.

beats.was: The US and Canada have put billions of dollars of tariffs on each other's goods in recent months, hurting Canadian steel and car makers. The Keystone XL pipeline, which would carry Canadian crude to the US, was cancelled in 2021.
beats.happened: Trump said he spoke with Carney by phone on Saturday and that the two sides have outlined a very good deal, with Canada paying to build the pipeline. Carney called the talks constructive but said negotiators will work on a framework over the coming weeks; no terms or tariff cuts were announced.
beats.means: It is the warmest tone in months, two days before the US midterm elections, but nothing is signed and Carney has said before that Canada will not rush into a bad deal.
beats.fx: Lower US tariffs would help Canada's exports and economy, which have stalled, so real progress would support the Canadian dollar; the market will want details first.

impact.why: Talk of a deal that could cut tariffs on Canadian goods helps, but there are no terms yet.

items.watch: Whether either side publishes terms, especially tariff relief on Canadian steel and cars.

items.headline: RBA Rate Hike Looms Amid Global Worries
items.story_title: Reserve Bank of Australia: a fifth rate rise this year?
items.summary: Economists expect the Reserve Bank of Australia to raise its rate on Tuesday, November 3, by a quarter point to 4.85%, and several think it will be the last rise of this run.

beats.was: Australia's central bank has raised its cash rate four times this year, to 4.60%, because inflation has stayed well above its target. Recent price figures came in hotter than expected.
beats.happened: Money markets now give a quarter-point rise a high chance at Tuesday's meeting, which would take the rate to 4.85%, among its highest in nearly two decades. The big Australian banks and several economists say this could be the peak.
beats.means: A rise is largely expected, so the Australian dollar's reaction will hang on what the bank says about the next step. A hint that this is the last rise could take some shine off the currency, and a surprise hold would hit it harder.
beats.fx: A hike with a firm tone would support the Australian dollar; a hold or a clear signal of a pause would weigh on it.

impact.why: An expected rate rise keeps Australian rates high, but it is mostly priced already.
The New Zealand dollar often moves with its neighbour's currency on Australian news.

items.watch: The decision and statement at 2:30 PM Australian east coast time on Tuesday (03:30 GMT), then the governor's news conference.

items.headline: Houthi media renews threats on Saudi oil giant, aviation
items.story_title: Yemen's Houthis vs Saudi Arabia
items.summary: Yemen's Houthi rebels, who are allied with Iran, warned again on Sunday that Saudi Aramco's oil sites are within their reach and told airlines to stay out of Saudi airspace.

beats.was: Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces restarted in July, and Houthi missiles and drones have since hit Saudi oil sites and airports, including a deadly strike on Riyadh's airport on October 10. A Saudi-led coalition struck Houthi supply sites in Yemen on Sunday morning.
beats.happened: An unnamed Houthi military official, quoted by the group's Saba news agency, said Aramco facilities are in range and investing in them is risky, and warned foreign airlines off Saudi airspace apart from over Mecca and Medina. No new attack was reported.
beats.means: It is a threat, not a strike, but it comes as the Saudi coalition hits back and Iran warns against new US attacks, so the risk to Saudi oil output stays live.
beats.fx: Any real damage to Saudi oil sites would add to oil prices that are already high because of the Gulf shipping attacks. Higher oil helps the Canadian dollar and hurts big oil importers like Japan and the euro zone.

impact.why: A repeated threat to the world's biggest oil exporter keeps supply worries up, though nothing new was hit.
Canada exports a lot of oil, so oil supply scares tend to help the loonie a little.

items.watch: Whether the Houthis follow through with a strike on Aramco sites, or the Saudi coalition's raids push them to escalate.

items.headline: Germany Misses Gas Storage Target as Cold Snap Sets In
items.story_title: Europe's gas: thin reserves going into winter
items.summary: Germany's gas stores were only about 61% full on November 1, short of its 70% goal, just as colder-than-usual weather arrives.

beats.was: Germany sets fill targets for its gas storage so it can get through winter, and European gas prices have roughly tripled this year because the Iran war cut Gulf supplies, topping €100 per megawatt-hour last week for the first time since 2022.
beats.happened: Data from Gas Infrastructure Europe showed German storage at 61% on Friday versus a 70% target, well below the EU average of 75%. The economy ministry admitted the target will be missed but said reserves should last the winter thanks to Norwegian pipelines and LNG terminals. Forecasts show temperatures below normal in Berlin, Frankfurt and Munich.
beats.means: Thin reserves plus a cold, possibly windless spell mean Germany may have to buy more gas at high prices, which raises costs for its factories and keeps energy inflation up.
beats.fx: Pricier energy hurts Europe's trade balance and growth, a weight on the euro, though it also keeps inflation high enough for the European Central Bank to consider raising rates.

impact.why: Low gas stores before a cold spell raise the euro zone's energy bill and the risk to German industry.

items.watch: How cold November turns out and whether European gas prices climb back above €100.

items.headline: Bank of England expected to raise interest rates to 4%
items.story_title: Bank of England's first rate rise since 2023
items.summary: Economists expect the Bank of England to lift its main rate from 3.75% to 4% on Thursday, November 5, its first rise since August 2023.

beats.was: UK inflation has stayed well above the Bank of England's 2% goal, and fuel costs have risen with the Middle East war. The household energy price cap went up 3.6% in October, and a far bigger rise is forecast for January.
beats.happened: Ahead of Thursday's decision, economists at Investec and the ICAEW, the accountants' body, said a quarter-point rise to 4% looks close to certain, framed as a move to stop high prices from becoming the norm.
beats.means: A rise is now the expected outcome, so it would confirm what markets already assume. What matters more is how many of the nine policymakers vote for it and whether the Bank hints at more.
beats.fx: The pound has gained on this expectation. A rise with signals of more could add to it, while a hold or a split vote that sounds reluctant would likely knock it.

impact.why: Higher UK rates support the pound, but the rise is largely priced in already.

items.watch: The vote split and the Bank's guidance on Thursday; a hold would be a real surprise.

items.headline: OPEC+ keeps December oil output targets steady ahead of tougher call for 2027
items.story_title: OPEC+ output: holding steady while war decides supply
items.summary: Seven leading OPEC+ oil producers confirmed on Sunday that their output targets stay unchanged for December; the harder decision on 2027 comes on November 29.

beats.was: OPEC+ is the group of oil exporters led by Saudi Arabia and Russia that sets production targets. The US-Iran war has disrupted Gulf exports for months, so most Gulf members are pumping well below their targets anyway.
beats.happened: In an online meeting on Sunday, Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman left December targets where they were, as they did for October and November. All 21 members meet on November 29 to set quotas for 2027.
beats.means: Nothing changes for now; actual supply still depends on how freely ships can pass the Strait of Hormuz. Forecasters warn of too much oil in 2027 if Gulf flows return to normal, which makes the November 29 meeting the one that matters.
beats.fx: Little direct effect on currencies this week. Oil prices, and with them the Canadian dollar and the yen's import bill, keep taking their lead from the war news.

impact.why: An expected hold; war disruptions, not quotas, are setting supply.
No change in output plans, so oil's support for Canada's currency rests on the war news.

items.watch: The OPEC+ meeting on November 29 that sets 2027 output, and the capacity review due by mid-November.

items.headline: Trump, Rubio say more Iran strikes are still on the table, but not likely before midterms
items.story_title: US-Iran talks and the threat of new strikes
items.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Trump has not decided whether to resume strikes on Iran and would rather reach a deal; Trump said talks are going fine.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since February, with a pause in fighting while Qatar mediates. Weekend reports said the US was preparing possible new strikes, and Iran has offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz on its own terms.
beats.happened: On Saturday, Rubio said Trump has made no decision on new strikes and prefers a diplomatic outcome. Trump called the talks fine but questioned how much Iran's negotiators can be trusted and said he is in no rush to sign. The report says new strikes look unlikely before Tuesday's US midterm elections.
beats.means: Washington is keeping both options open: talks continue in Doha while strikes stay possible. The near-term risk of fresh fighting looks a little lower, but nothing is settled.
beats.fx: A pause in the threat of strikes takes a little of the war premium out of oil and eases shelter demand for the Swiss franc. A collapse of the talks would quickly reverse that.

impact.why: Talk of preferring a deal trims the odds of fighting in the next few days.
Less immediate war risk means less need for the franc as shelter.

items.watch: Whether the US answers Iran's two-day Hormuz offer, and any move toward strikes after Tuesday's midterm elections.

items.headline: Mediators continue US-Iran negotiations amid war rhetoric: What we know
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: A letter from US Vice President JD Vance has softened the tone between Washington and Tehran, even as both sides prepare for possible new fighting.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since late February, and a June truce brokered by Qatar and Pakistan fell apart in August. The two mediators are trying to restart talks.
beats.happened: Vance wrote this week to Mohsen Rezaei, a senior Iranian security official, who said the letter's tone was completely different from earlier US messages and claimed Washington was ready to accept Iran's terms. The US has not confirmed that. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said talks go on with no timeline, while Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei told commanders to widen their list of targets.
beats.means: Both tracks are running at once: a warmer channel for talks and open preparation for another short round of strikes after the US midterm elections on November 3. Neither side has committed to either path.
beats.fx: A real opening in talks would ease oil prices and help oil importers like Japan and the euro zone. Renewed strikes would do the opposite and lift shelter currencies like the Swiss franc.

impact.why: A friendlier US letter points toward talks, but both sides are also readying for more fighting.
Shelter demand rises or fades depending on which track wins.

items.watch: Whether the US confirms Iran's claim that it will accept Tehran's terms, and any strike decision after November 3.

items.headline: Araghchi says Hormuz could be reopened within two days if conditions met
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Iran's foreign minister says the Strait of Hormuz could reopen within two days, but only if the US first meets a long list of demands.

beats.was: The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that carries about a fifth of the world's oil, has been largely shut by the US-Iran war, and tankers keep catching fire there. Qatar has been carrying messages between the two sides.
beats.happened: On Sunday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said a plan worked out with Qatari mediators would let the strait reopen on day two if Washington acts on day one. His conditions include lifting US sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian money, restoring oil waivers, pulling back US forces and ending fighting on all fronts.
beats.means: It is an offer, not a deal. The demands are ones Washington has not accepted before, so it shows a path to reopening rather than a sign one is near.
beats.fx: A reopened strait would pull oil prices down, which helps big oil buyers like Japan and hurts oil exporters like Canada. For now the price of oil still carries the war risk.

impact.why: A stated path to reopening the main oil sea lane, though only on terms the US has refused so far.
Japan buys nearly all its oil abroad, so any route to cheaper oil eases pressure on the yen.

items.watch: Whether Washington answers the offer, and whether US strikes resume after the November 3 midterm elections.

items.headline: Two oil tankers explode after hitting mine in Hormuz Strait, IRGC says
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two oil tankers hit Iranian sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, leaving one supertanker on fire, while a UK shipping-security agency reported another tanker struck by an unknown projectile.

beats.was: The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that carries about a fifth of the world's oil, has been largely shut since the US-Iran war began in February, and ships trying to pass have been mined, shot at or seized. Several tankers were hit last week.
beats.happened: A spokesman for the Guards' navy told Iranian state TV the two tankers took an unapproved route with their tracking systems off and blamed their owners. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said a tanker was hit by an unknown object earlier on Sunday. None of this has been independently confirmed.
beats.means: Ships keep getting hit even as Iran and the US talk through Qatar, so the few routes still open look riskier and insurance and freight costs stay high.
beats.fx: More damage to Gulf shipping supports oil prices, which helps oil exporters like Canada and hurts big importers such as Japan and the euro zone.

impact.why: Two more tankers hit in the main Gulf oil lane raises the risk that even less crude gets out.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, so a higher import bill weighs on the yen.
Canada sells a lot of oil, so Gulf supply scares tend to lift the loonie a little.

items.watch: Whether Monday's oil trading opens higher, and whether the US Navy or shipping agencies confirm the Iranian account.

items.headline: China's regulators to meet banks on Monday on steps to steady stocks after an October slump
items.story_title: China's slowdown and Beijing's response
items.summary: China's central bank and its market and banking regulators meet big banks and fund firms on Monday to discuss more support for a stock market that slid hard in October.

beats.was: Chinese shares had a bad October: the Shanghai index fell about 6% and the tech-heavy Shenzhen index about 16%, with the main growth boards down over 23%. Official figures on Saturday also showed factory and service activity shrinking.
beats.happened: Mainland media reported on Sunday that the People's Bank of China, the China Securities Regulatory Commission and the National Financial Regulatory Administration will meet major banks and fund companies on Monday, November 2. They are expected to discuss widening cheap loans that help companies and big holders buy back shares.
beats.means: Beijing is signalling it will not let the sell-off run unchecked. A meeting is not yet new money, so the effect depends on what measures come out of it.
beats.fx: Steadier Chinese markets help currencies tied to China's demand, chiefly the Australian and New Zealand dollars. If the steps disappoint, the weak October figures would weigh again.

impact.why: Support for Chinese stocks eases worry about Australia's biggest customer, but no measures are announced yet.
China is a major buyer of New Zealand's exports, so steadier Chinese markets help a little.

items.watch: What the Monday meeting in Beijing announces, and China's private-sector factory survey the same day.

items.headline: Qatar LNG tanker struck in Gulf: crew safe, no oil spill reported
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: A Qatari tanker carrying liquefied natural gas was hit by unidentified objects in the Gulf on Friday evening; the crew is safe and the ship still works.

beats.was: Gulf shipping has been under attack since the US-Iran war began in February, and Iran says ships need its permission to pass the Strait of Hormuz. Qatar is one of the world's biggest gas exporters and is also mediating between Washington and Tehran.
beats.happened: Qatar's state news agency said on Sunday that the Al Mayeda, a gas carrier run by Qatari shipper Nakilat, was struck while sailing in the Gulf on Friday, October 30. No one was hurt, nothing leaked and the ship remains in service. No one has said who was behind it.
beats.means: The attacks are no longer limited to oil tankers, and this one hit a ship from the country trying to broker peace. Damage was light, so supply is not affected for now.
beats.fx: More risk to Gulf gas shipments would push up energy costs for big gas buyers in Europe and Asia, a weight on the euro and the yen. It also keeps oil prices carrying a war premium.

impact.why: Another ship hit in the Gulf keeps shipping risk high, though damage was light.
Europe relies on imported gas, so threats to Gulf gas cargoes raise its energy bill.

items.watch: Whether attacks on gas carriers continue and whether insurers or shippers start avoiding Qatari routes.

items.headline: Trump holds call with Netanyahu amid preparations to renew strikes on Iran -- report
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: The US is preparing for possible new strikes on Iran, with Gulf allies reportedly warned they could come as soon as November 4, while talks carry on.

beats.was: The US has not struck Iran since September 1, and talks run through Qatar. Washington has been telling Gulf partners to get ready for action after Tuesday's US midterm elections.
beats.happened: President Donald Trump spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday, The Wall Street Journal reported, and said the US still needs to deal with "one or two sites" in Iran. One report says Gulf allies were warned of strikes as early as November 4. A top Iranian security official said Tehran is debating whether to drop its ban on nuclear weapons if fighting resumes.
beats.means: The risk of the war flaring up again in the coming days has gone up, even as both sides keep talking. Trump still says talks are going fine.
beats.fx: Fresh fighting would likely push oil higher and send money into shelter currencies like the Swiss franc. It would hurt big oil importers such as Japan and the euro zone.

impact.why: Reports of strike preparations raise the odds of new fighting near the main oil sea lane.
War risk tends to draw shelter money into the franc.
The euro zone imports most of its energy, so a jump in oil would weigh on it.

items.watch: Any US decision on strikes after the November 3 midterm elections, and any reply to Iran's two-day reopening offer.

items.headline: OPEC+ set to keep oil output targets steady, sources say
items.story_title: OPEC+: oil output targets
items.summary: The OPEC+ oil producers are set to keep their December output targets unchanged at an online meeting on Sunday, a third month without change.

beats.was: OPEC+ is the group of oil producers led by Saudi Arabia and Russia. It finished undoing one round of output cuts in September and kept its targets unchanged for October and November.
beats.happened: Three sources told Reuters the seven core members agreed in principle on Saturday to leave December targets alone, with the formal decision due at an online meeting on Sunday. Changes are not expected until next year, after a review of how much each member can pump.
beats.means: No surprise here. Gulf members are still pumping well below their targets because the Iran war has disrupted their exports, so the targets matter less than the war right now.
beats.fx: A steady OPEC+ leaves oil, and the currencies tied to it like the Canadian dollar and the Norwegian krone, driven by news from the Strait of Hormuz.

impact.why: An expected hold that changes little while war disruptions decide supply.

items.watch: The formal statement from Sunday's meeting and any hint about 2027 quotas.

items.headline: Coalition destroys drone over Riyadh, Khamenei warns US
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Iran's Supreme Leader warned that any new US or Israeli attack would meet a reply with no geographic limits, the same day Saudi air defenses shot down a drone near the capital, Riyadh.

beats.was: The US has not struck Iran since September 1 and indirect talks continue through Qatar, but Washington is weighing new strikes after Tuesday's US midterm elections. Yemen's Houthi rebels, who are backed by Iran, have stepped up attacks on Saudi oil sites.
beats.happened: On Saturday, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said in a statement that any fresh attack would be answered anywhere, and reportedly told the armed forces to update their lists of US and Israeli targets. Separately, the Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed a drone over the Riyadh area; debris fell but no one was hurt, and no group was named.
beats.means: Iran is signalling that a new round of strikes would not stay contained, which raises the cost of escalation for everyone in the Gulf. These are words and a single intercepted drone, not new damage to oil supply.
beats.fx: A wider war would likely lift oil and draw shelter money into the Swiss franc, while hurting big energy importers like Japan and the euro zone. For now it mostly adds to worry already in prices.

impact.why: Threats of a reply with no limits raise the risk to Gulf oil routes and facilities if fighting resumes.
Rising war talk tends to draw shelter money into the franc.

items.watch: Whether the US decides on new strikes after the November 3 midterms, and any fresh attacks on Saudi or Gulf energy sites.

items.headline: Chinese NBS Manufacturing PMI (Oct) 49.3 vs. Exp. 50 (Prev. 50.1)
items.story_title: China: a slowing economy
items.summary: China's official business surveys for October fell below the 50 line that splits growth from shrinking, for both factories and services, and both missed forecasts.

beats.was: China's National Bureau of Statistics publishes monthly purchasing managers' surveys, where readings above 50 mean activity is growing. In September both factories (50.1) and services and construction (50.2) were just above that line.
beats.happened: On Saturday the factory reading dropped to 49.3, against 50.0 expected, and the services and construction reading fell to 49.7, against 50.5 expected. The combined measure slid to 49.7 from 50.7, with weak demand, including for exports, blamed.
beats.means: The world's second-largest economy slipped back into shrinking across the board in October, with costly oil and softer overseas orders weighing. It raises the odds Beijing adds more support.
beats.fx: China buys much of Australia's iron ore and much of New Zealand's dairy, so a weaker China tends to weigh on both their currencies, and on demand for oil and metals.

impact.why: China is Australia's biggest customer, and both factory and service activity there shrank more than expected.
Softer Chinese demand is a worry for New Zealand's exports.
Shrinking Chinese activity trims hopes for oil demand, though war supply worries dominate for now.

items.watch: China's private-sector surveys early next week and any sign Beijing steps up spending or rate cuts.

items.headline: Oil jumps 2pc
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: Oil closed Friday at its highest since late April and gained about 14% in October, as traders braced for the Iran war to flare again after next week's US elections.

beats.was: Oil has climbed for four months as the war with Iran disrupts Gulf shipping, even though Gulf exports have recovered by sending more crude around the Strait of Hormuz.
beats.happened: Brent crude for December, which expired on Friday, settled up 2.4% at $117.64 a barrel after touching $118; US crude settled near $104. Brent rose 13.6% over October and US crude 15.2%. Maritime sources called a tanker hit by a small boat's explosives the first successful limpet-mine attack in the strait since the war began.
beats.means: Oil is ending the month near its highs, with traders paying up in case fighting resumes after the November 3 midterms. Qatari mediators are back in Tehran, but Iran has yet to answer a US letter.
beats.fx: Dear oil supports Canada's dollar and keeps pressure on oil importers such as Japan and the euro zone, while feeding inflation worries that keep rate-rise talk alive.

impact.why: Prices closed at a six-month high on fears of new fighting after the midterms.
Higher crude prices help Canada's export earnings.
A bigger oil import bill weighs on Japan.

items.watch: Any reply from Iran to the US letter, and tanker traffic through the strait when markets reopen.

items.headline: IRGC says fourth tanker hit mine in Strait of Hormuz
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a fourth tanker in a single day caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, a supertanker carrying over 2 million barrels, and Britain's maritime agency reported a separate ship hit by a projectile.

beats.was: Since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in February, Iran has limited traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea route for much of the world's oil, and says ships must use routes it approves.
beats.happened: Late on Friday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards navy said a supertanker leaving by a southern route it calls unauthorised struck a mine and caught fire, the fourth tanker fire since Friday began. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said an unknown projectile hit a ship about 40 nautical miles south of Iran's Lavan Island; the crew was safe.
beats.means: Iran is showing it can still threaten ships that defy it, even as the US says it has cleared Iranian mines from the strait. Each new attack lifts insurance and freight costs for Gulf oil.
beats.fx: More danger to Gulf shipping supports oil prices, which helps oil exporters like Canada and hurts big importers like Japan, and it can draw money into havens such as the Swiss franc.

impact.why: Repeated tanker strikes in the main Gulf export route keep supply fears high.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so dearer crude hurts its trade balance.
Rising war risk tends to draw shelter money to the franc.
Higher oil prices help Canada, a big crude exporter.

items.watch: Whether shipping firms confirm the strikes, and whether tanker traffic through the strait slows over the weekend.

items.headline: Fitch revises France's outlook to 'negative' on worsening debt dynamics
items.story_title: France: rising debt and a budget fight
items.summary: Credit rating agency Fitch warned it may cut France's rating, changing its outlook to negative because debt keeps climbing and politics make cuts hard.

beats.was: France is struggling to pass next year's budget amid street protests, its economy shrank last quarter, and its 10-year borrowing cost rose above 5.1% last week, the highest since 2002.
beats.happened: Late on Friday Fitch moved France's outlook from stable to negative, pointing to weaker growth, higher borrowing costs and a wider deficit since August. It expects debt to reach about 124% of the economy by 2028, up from about 116% last year.
beats.means: A negative outlook is a warning that a downgrade could follow. It adds pressure on French bonds just as Paris needs to show it can cut its deficit before the next presidential election.
beats.fx: Worry about France's debt can push its borrowing costs up relative to Germany's, which tends to weigh on the euro, though the effect is usually small unless a downgrade actually comes.

impact.why: A step toward a French downgrade adds to doubts about the euro zone's second-largest economy.

items.watch: How French bonds trade on Monday after weekend protests, and whether the budget makes it through parliament.

items.headline: THE CLOSING BELL: Wall Street drops to its worst day since June after the sell-off for tech stocks deepens
items.story_title: Wall Street: doubts over AI spending
items.summary: US stocks had their worst day since June on Friday as doubts about the payoff from heavy AI spending spread, while investors bought government bonds and pushed yields lower.

beats.was: Big US tech firms have been spending huge sums on AI data centres, and this week's earnings from Alphabet, Amazon and Intel raised doubts about when that spending pays off.
beats.happened: The S&P 500 fell 1.8%, a third weekly loss, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 2.9%. Intel dropped about 29%, its worst day since 1974, after a weak forecast. The 10-year US Treasury yield slipped to 4.93%, down from above 5.30% earlier in October.
beats.means: Fear is spreading from a few AI names to the wider market just before Tuesday's US midterm elections. Falling bond yields show money hiding in safer assets.
beats.fx: Lower US yields take away some of the dollar's rate support, while stock-market stress usually helps the yen and the Swiss franc and hurts riskier currencies like the Australian dollar.

impact.why: Stock-market stress and lower US yields tend to help the yen.
Lower yields weigh on the dollar, but shelter demand for US bonds pulls the other way.
A broad stock sell-off tends to draw money to the franc.
The Australian dollar usually falls when global stocks slide.

items.watch: Whether the sell-off spreads in Asia on Monday and how markets treat Tuesday's midterm results.

items.headline: Fed needs at least two more rate hikes, Logan says
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, who votes on rates this year, said the Fed should raise rates at least twice more, by a quarter point each, and then pause to take stock.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve kept its rate at 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday in a 10-2 vote, and Chair Kevin Warsh declined to promise a rise in December even after strong growth and inflation figures.
beats.happened: Logan, who backed Wednesday's hold, told students at Davidson College that rates should end at least half a point higher to bring inflation back to 2%, and that skipping one meeting does not change where policy is heading. Earlier in the day St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said a rise is needed soon.
beats.means: Two policymakers in one day are now pushing for more rises, and Logan put a number on it, which makes a December rise and at least one more after it easier to price.
beats.fx: A higher path for US rates supports the dollar and weighs on gold, though falling bond yields on stock-market worries blunted the effect on Friday.

impact.why: A voting Fed official calling for two more rises firms up the case for higher US rates.
Higher expected US rates make gold, which pays no interest, less attractive.

items.watch: If Warsh or other voters push back on a set path, or US jobs figures next week come in weak, the case for two more rises fades.

items.headline: Gold Crashes Below $3,900 to One-Year Low Even as Global Stock Markets Plunge
items.story_title: Gold: sliding as Fed rate-rise bets build
items.summary: Gold fell about 3% on Friday to just under $3,900 an ounce, its lowest in a year, even as stocks sold off, which would normally help it.

beats.was: Gold peaked near $5,600 in January and had been drifting lower as hot US inflation figures raised the odds of another Federal Reserve rate rise in December.
beats.happened: Spot gold dropped about 3.1% to roughly $3,897, leaving it some 30% below its record; silver fell about 6% to under $50 for the first time in nearly a year. Analysts quoted by Reuters suggested some investors sold gold to cover losses on falling tech shares.
beats.means: Rising US rate expectations and oil-driven inflation worries are outweighing gold's usual pull as a safe place in a sell-off, and forced selling made the drop sharper.
beats.fx: Clear pressure on gold; the selling is about higher US rates rather than a stronger dollar, which was softer on the day.

impact.why: A one-year low on bets for higher US rates and selling to cover stock losses.

items.watch: If US stocks steady and the margin-call selling stops, or Fed officials soften their talk of more rises, gold could find a floor.

items.headline: Fed's Musalem says a rate hike is needed 'soon'
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said the Fed will need to raise rates again, and soon, because inflation is still too high.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve held its rate at 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday after a rise in September, and Chair Kevin Warsh would not say what comes in December.
beats.happened: Musalem, who does not vote on rates this year but will next year, said in a speech that policy is still too loose to bring inflation down to 2% and that small, early rises are safer than bigger ones later.
beats.means: He adds his voice to the officials pushing for a December rise, and argues it can be done without hurting jobs or growth.
beats.fx: Talk of more Fed rises supports the dollar, though on Friday a stock sell-off pulling bond yields lower largely offset it.

impact.why: Another Fed official backing a near-term rise supports US rates, but he has no vote this year.
Higher expected US rates make gold, which pays no interest, less appealing.

items.watch: The US jobs report on November 6; a weak one would make a December rise harder to argue for.
